forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Hyndburn pushes ahead with £30m housing scheme as government pauses reorganisation plan
news_drafts.lead: Hyndburn cabinet has approved plans to deliver a £29.898 million infrastructure programme for the Huncoat Garden Village, funded by central government through the Brownfield, Infrastructure and Land Fund. The scheme will unlock 1,816 new homes and includes land remediation, a relief road and contributions to the M65 Junction 8. Spending will peak at £20.1 million in 2027/28. Separately, the council faces an uncertain future after the government halted its nationwide Local Government Reorganisation programme on 7 September, leaving Hyndburn's proposed merger into a Pennine Lancashire unitary authority on hold. Finance staff have already diverted resources to preparatory work. The council is also managing costs at town centre projects funded through the £20 million Levelling Up Fund, completing November 2026, with both the new Market Hall and Burtons Chambers requiring careful monitoring until trading performance stabilises.

news_drafts.headline: Hyndburn removed Cabinet members from Audit Committee but failed to appoint two independent members agreed in June 2024
news_drafts.lead: Hyndburn Council has improved the independence of its Audit Committee by removing Cabinet members from it, bringing the body into line with guidance from the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA). However, the council agreed in June 2024 to appoint two independent members to the Committee and has made no progress in the two years since. The Executive Director for Legal and Democratic Services told the Committee in September that the appointment process had stalled because of competing corporate priorities and preparations for Local Government Reorganisation. The Committee heard that the next step — reporting to the Leaders Policy Board — has not yet taken place. An Audit Committee with independent members, separate from Cabinet, is intended to strengthen oversight of the council's finances and governance.

news_drafts.headline: Hyndburn council faces £845,000 four-year funding gap for local plan delivery
news_drafts.lead: Hyndburn council has identified a £844,800 shortfall over four years to fund its local plan — the blueprint for where homes and businesses can be built — after government grant funding ends next year. The council is spending an estimated £970,000 to produce the plan, covering staff, environmental assessments and public consultation, but has only £125,200 available. A one-off government grant of £108,000 runs until 2026/27; after that, the council's regular budget of £4,300 a year will fall far short of the estimated £95,000 to £475,000 needed annually. In the 2027/28 financial year alone, the council faces a shortfall of £470,700. The council has flagged the gap in its budget papers but has not yet committed additional funding. Internal audit opinion improved slightly in 2025/26, though a payroll system audit received limited assurance, indicating some control weaknesses.

findings.headline: Hyndburn expected to receive less government funding by end of 2028/29 settlement period than under 2025/26 baseline, with limited council tax base capacity to offset reductions.
findings.detail: Final Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27–2028/29 published February 2026. Although national Core Spending Power increased, Hyndburn's limited council tax base and weak tax-raising capacity make it difficult to offset reductions in grant funding. Sources of pressure include end of New Homes Bonus, grant consolidation and changes to retained business rates. Transitional protection provided but does not eliminate underlying pressure.
findings.matters: Finance directors track funding trajectory and the sustainability of medium-term financial strategies.
findings.figures: Expected funding reduction by end of settlement period versus 2025/26 baseline
findings.quote: Based on current settlement information and Council modelling, Hyndburn is expected to receive less funding than under the 2025/26 baseline by the end of the settlement period.

findings.headline: Up to £400,000 per annum recurring funding gap identified for 2027/28 onwards as staff posts currently funded from reserves or external grants lose their funding.
findings.detail: Several council staff posts currently sustained through reserves or external grants will lose funding from 2027/28. Up to £400,000 per annum required to maintain them. Pressure already built into Medium-Term Financial Strategy projections. Officers actively exploring new funding opportunities to reduce impact.
findings.matters: Finance directors track recurring budget pressures and the sustainability of positions funded outside base budgets.
findings.quote: Several staff posts that are currently funded through reserves, or external grants could face a funding shortfall from 2027/28, with up to £400,000 per annum required to sustain them.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy losses from Supported Exempt Accommodation declining—£525,000 (2024/25), £499,000 (2025/26), £436,000 forecast (2026/27 mid-year)—but remain volatile and unpredictable without continued regulatory oversight.
findings.detail: Council concerned about financial challenges from non-registered providers of Supported Exempt Accommodation, where Housing Benefit subsidy is significantly reduced, creating direct financial burden. Council adoption of Article 4 planning control provides stronger management mechanism. Losses showing clear improvement trend but subsidy stream remains volatile and difficult to predict.
findings.matters: Finance directors track welfare-dependent income streams and monitor volatility in subsidy-driven funding.
findings.figures: 2024/25 actual loss: £525,000; 2025/26 actual loss: £499,000; 2026/27 mid-year forecast: £436,000
findings.quote: Supported Housing costs have stabilised, and the subsidy losses look to be gradually reducing to: 2024/25 Year-End: Actual subsidy loss of £525k; 2025/26 Year-End: Actual subsidy loss of £499k; 2026/27 Mid-Year: Forecast loss of £436k.

findings.headline: Market Hall assumed self-financing from 2027/28 and Burtons Chambers supported by two-year £450,000 reserve allocation; both remain financial risks until trading performance is established.
findings.detail: £20 million Levelling Up Fund town centre projects completing November 2026, operational from 2027/28. Market Hall requires £605,000 additional set-up costs to be funded from existing reserves and capital savings, with assumption of self-financing from 2027/28 onwards. Burtons Chambers has £450,000 set aside from reserves for two years' operating costs. Both have material revenue cost risks during ramp-up period if operating costs exceed income.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to track new operational commitments and untested revenue assumptions emerging from capital projects.
findings.figures: £20,000,000 Levelling Up Fund; £605,000 Market Hall setup costs; £450,000 Burtons Chambers operating reserve
findings.quote: For the Market Hall, the current assumption is that the development will be self-financing from 2027/28. This assumption remains a financial risk until tested through actual trading and will be closely monitored throughout the financial year.

findings.headline: £29.898 million Homes England funded Huncoat Garden Village infrastructure programme in delivery phase, with peak expenditure of £20.1 million forecast for 2027/28; cost overruns not absorbed by developers fall to council.
findings.detail: Council is delivering major infrastructure programme following award of £29.898 million from Homes England's Brownfield, Infrastructure and Land Fund. Spend to date: £3.6 million; 2026/27 forecast: £3.5 million; 2027/28 forecast: £20.1 million; 2028/29 forecast: £2.7 million. Programme includes land remediation, relief road and M65 Junction 8 contributions; will unlock 1,816 homes. Key risk: cost overruns not absorbed or passed to developers would fall on council.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track major capital programmes, expenditure profiles and contingent liabilities.
findings.figures: £29.898 million total funded; £3.6 million spend to date; £3.5 million (2026/27), £20.1 million (2027/28), £2.7 million (2028/29) forecast; 1,816 homes capacity
findings.quote: Following the award of £29.898 million from Homes England's Brownfield, Infrastructure and Land (BIL) Fund, the Council is now in the delivery phase of a major infrastructure programme.
